passes.name: Pass 1
passes.note: First router run, after the power pours and Kelvin taps were drawn from coordinates.

passes.name: Pass 2
passes.note: Same placement, failed nets routed first.

passes.name: Pass 3
passes.note: Another net order. Conclusion: order is not the problem, the parts sit too tight for pins to reach a via.

passes.name: Pass 4
passes.note: Parts placed again with a clear ring round each fine-pitch IC. Inner layers allowed to jog off their preferred direction.

passes.name: Pass 5
passes.note: Rip-up and re-route added to the router.

passes.name: Pass 6
passes.note: Placement fixed at the PD EEPROM, the second protector and a few charger pins, where fixed parts boxed nets in.

passes.name: Pass 7
passes.note: Long top-to-bottom nets routed first. The full rule check then found 71 spacing errors: the router applied the high-current rule one way round only.

passes.name: Pass 8
passes.note: Router fixed and those tracks laid again (71 errors down to 3), which opened ten connections again. A pour was covering the only via site for one pad.

passes.name: Pass 9
passes.note: Last nets with hand-specified routes, the cut-up planes joined again. Then widening, silkscreen, final rule check and cup fit by 10:39.

passes.name: Fix pass, first board
passes.note: Gate drives and the signals near switching copper lifted and laid again, four capacitors moved, vias added, six nets onto inner layer 4. It passed every check, and the comparison then found the PACK_P bus cut and the battery sense taps touched.

passes.name: Fix pass, final
passes.note: Both faults corrected. Port 2 feedback track, the TS4 line and both charger TS vias moved away from the switch nodes.

tools: Loads and saves the board through its Python interface, refills zones, runs the rule check with the project's own rules and the schematic parity check, renders the pictures.
Stock KiCad. No autorouter product was used.
Part positions kept as one JSON file and applied to the board, so a placement can be changed and replayed.
Moves each part's 3D mesh to its new position and runs the 26 checks of the mechanical model after every placement change.
The checks were in the repo; the runner is new
Draw the power pours, via fields and Kelvin taps from coordinates I worked out per net.
A* maze router on a 0.05 mm grid over the front, back and two inner layers. Knows the clearance classes, escapes fine-pitch pins, rips up and re-routes, adds ground stitching. 1,641 lines.
Finds pieces of the GND, 3V3 and PACK_P planes that a new track cut off. KiCad only shows those as one airwire.
Small JSON files with exact tracks and vias for the spots the router could not solve, plus helpers that list free via sites and draw a zoomed picture of a pocket.
Exact-clearance shortest-path search for one connection at a time over the signal layers, and a second one for single-layer tracks inside a ground plane.
Path resistance, loss maps, via currents and Kelvin tap error from the real copper.
Coupling capacitance from each switch node to every other net.
Shows where on a net the charge from a switch node sits, in 0.5 mm bins per layer, so the track or via to move is known.
Added to the field solver in the fix pass
Loss at each load and the temperature runs. The 12 thermal runs ran on your PC.
The layout rules I started from and the routing-discipline checker.
Python with numpy, scipy, pyamg, Pillow, matplotlib; a headless browser
All the solvers and pictures; the browser to look at this page before publishing it.
